name: Papermaking in Samarkand and Abbasid Baghdad
summary: Paper and papermaking passed from Central Asia into the Abbasid lands, where by the early ninth century Baghdad's officials kept records on it, and on to North Africa and Spain.
description: Muslims first met paper in Central Asia in the eighth century, where it was already in use: paper documents were found at Mount Mug near Panjakent, a stronghold linked to events of 722-723. An eleventh-century writer, al-Tha'alibi, credited Chinese prisoners taken at Talas in 751 with bringing papermaking to Samarkand, an account Bloom does not take at face value. By the reign of Harun al-Rashid (786-809) Baghdad had enough paper for officials to keep records on it instead of papyrus and parchment. Papermakers in the Islamic lands came to use waste rags and old rope as fibre and to dip the mould in a vat of pulp, and the craft spread to Syria, Egypt, North Africa and Spain.

impact.note: Paper made in the Islamic lands became the ordinary writing material from Central Asia to Spain, and Bloom traces European papermaking to it, so the paper of nearly every region outside East Asia descends from this transmission (reach 3); it replaced papyrus and parchment, and administration, commerce and book-copying were reorganised around it (depth 2); the papermaking, stationery and book trades of the Islamic world and then of Europe grew from it (generativity 2).

why: According to Ibn Khaldun, as reported by Bloom, the vizier al-Fadl ibn Yahya introduced paper manufacture to Baghdad when parchment was in short supply and he needed more writing materials.

date.label: soon after 751 CE (as claimed in the 11th century)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: According to the later writer al-Tha'alibi, Chinese prisoners captured at the battle of Talas in 751 introduced papermaking to Samarkand afterwards; this is his claim, not a contemporary record.

evidence.supports: According to al-Tha'alibi, Chinese prisoners captured by the Arab commander Ziyad ibn Salih introduced papermaking to Samarkand after the battle of Talas in 751.

date.label: by 809 CE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: By the reign of Harun al-Rashid (786-809), enough paper was available in Baghdad for bureaucrats to use it for records instead of papyrus and parchment.

evidence.supports: By the reign of the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid (786-809), enough paper was available in Baghdad for bureaucrats to use it for record-keeping instead of papyrus and parchment.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

links.statement: Paper and the knowledge of making it travelled from China to Central Asia, where Muslims first met it in the eighth century.

evidence.supports: Chinese merchants and missionaries transmitted paper, and knowledge of papermaking, to neighboring lands such as Japan, Korea, and Central Asia. It was there that Muslims first encountered it in the eighth century.

unresolved.note: Confirm the first Baghdad paper mill (c. 794-795) from a scholarly source on early Islamic papermaking; the fetched article does not give it.

Check Bloom's Paper Before Print for the Talas critique, the Mount Mug dating and when rag fibre and vat dipping replaced older methods; this card takes all three from his Aramco World article, which dates none of the process changes.
When papermaking reached al-Andalus and Italy needs dated primary sources; the article's 1056 for a mill at Játiva is disputed elsewhere and was not used.
Whether paper was made at Samarkand before 751; the Mount Mug documents show paper in use near there by 722-723 but not where it was made.

research.note: Bloom writes that paper was undoubtedly introduced to the Middle East through Central Asia, and that the Arabic word kaghad, from Soghdian and Uighur words that derive from Chinese, confirms that route from China.
